title: Prince Igor: Polovtsian Dances
hook: A captive prince, a khan’s feast and a melody that later became “Stranger in Paradise”.

painting.title: After Prince Igor’s Battle with the Polovtsy
painting.pairingNote: Russian warriors lie dead on the steppe after Igor’s defeat of 1185, the battle that makes him the Khan’s prisoner in Borodin’s opera; Vasnetsov painted it from the same medieval epic while Borodin was still at work on the music.

facts: *Prince Igor* was Borodin’s great opera project. He took the story from *The Lay of Igor’s Campaign*, a medieval Russian epic about a prince who rode out against the Polovtsy, nomads of the southern steppe, in 1185, was defeated and taken prisoner. The critic Vladimir Stasov suggested the subject in 1869.

Borodin was a professor of chemistry first and a composer in his spare time, and he worked on the opera, on and off, for almost eighteen years. When he died suddenly in 1887 it was still unfinished. Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Glazunov completed and orchestrated it, and it was first staged in St Petersburg in 1890.

The dances end Act 2 (Act 1 in some versions). In the Polovtsian camp Khan Konchak treats his captive Igor as an honoured guest, and calls his slaves to dance and sing for him while the Polovtsy sing the Khan’s praises.

The dances were ready long before the opera. For a concert in 1879 Rimsky-Korsakov, who was rehearsing the chorus, lost patience and helped Borodin and Anatoly Lyadov orchestrate them in a single night. They wrote in pencil, and Borodin coated the pages with gelatine and hung them up to dry like washing.
bigPicture.inOneLine: the slave girls’ longing song (I), the men’s wild dance (II), praise of the Khan (III), the boys’ dance (IV), the girls’ song again (V), the boys once more (VI) and everyone together (VII).

movements.heading: Introduction – Gliding Dance of the Maidens
movements.title: Introduction – Gliding Dance of the Maidens
movements.summary: A soft, shimmering introduction, then one of the most famous melodies in Russian music: a slow, curving tune with a touch of the East, first in the oboe and then in the cor anglais. The captive women take it up. They sing of their homeland, asking their song to fly there on the wings of the wind.

mainIdeas.name: The maidens’ melody
mainIdeas.description: long, swaying and sad, with ornaments that curl around the main notes. In 1953 the Broadway musical *Kismet* turned it into the song “Stranger in Paradise”.

stops.hear: Soft woodwind phrases over quiet, sustained strings
stops.happening: The introduction: evening in the camp

stops.hear: The oboe plays a slow, curving melody
stops.happening: The gliding dance of the slave girls

stops.hear: The cor anglais, darker and lower, answers with the same tune
stops.happening: The melody in a new colour

stops.hear: The women’s voices take up the melody
stops.happening: “Fly away on the wings of the wind”: their song to the homeland

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The tune fades out quietly

notice: Listen to the ornaments in the oboe’s tune, the little turns around the main notes. They are what gives it its Eastern colour.

movements.heading: Wild Dance of the Men
movements.title: Wild Dance of the Men
movements.summary: The calm breaks. A clarinet races off on a fast, whirling tune over a hammering accompaniment, and the whole orchestra joins in: the Polovtsian warriors leap into their dance.

mainIdeas.name: The men’s tune
mainIdeas.description: fast, twisting runs for the clarinet, then for the whole orchestra, over an insistent, drumming [[ostinato|ostinato]].

stops.hear: A clarinet races off on a fast, swirling tune
The full orchestra takes over, with the percussion

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: The music winds up and stops abruptly

notice: Notice how short this dance is. It is a burst of energy rather than a dance with a beginning and an end.

movements.heading: General Dance
movements.title: General Dance
movements.summary: The whole chorus enters. In a heavy, swinging three-beat rhythm, with crashing percussion, the Polovtsy sing the praises of their Khan, Konchak. It is music of pomp and power, and Igor, the captive, must sit and listen to it.

mainIdeas.name: The praise of the Khan
mainIdeas.description: a broad, swinging tune in three beats, sung by the full chorus over a pounding orchestra.

stops.hear: A loud outburst in a swinging three-beat rhythm
The full chorus sings
The tune comes round again, even louder

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Crashing chords

notice: Listen to the percussion marking the heavy three beats, like a court ceremony.

movements.heading: Dance of the Boys
movements.title: Dance of the Boys
movements.summary: A sudden change of speed: a very fast dance in a skipping rhythm, light and brilliant, for the Polovtsian boys. Then the men come in again, with the chorus, in a heavier version of the same idea.

mainIdeas.name: The boys’ dance
mainIdeas.description: quick, skipping notes in a fast six-beat rhythm, in the minor.

stops.hear: Very fast, light, skipping music
The music grows heavier and louder, and voices join in

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A sharp stop
stops.happening: The pause before the maidens return

notice: Tap the rhythm: it goes in two big beats, each split into three quick ones, like a gallop.

movements.heading: Gliding Dance of the Maidens
movements.title: Gliding Dance of the Maidens
movements.summary: The maidens’ melody returns, now in a major key and moving a little faster. Soon the boys’ quick figures begin to run underneath it, and the two dances are heard at once.

mainIdeas.description: The maidens’ melody combined with the boys’ rhythm: Borodin’s trick of making two themes fit together.

stops.hear: The slow, curving melody of the first dance, brighter now
Quick, skipping figures begin to run beneath the melody
stops.happening: The boys’ dance joins the maidens’ song

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The texture thickens and the speed rises

notice: Listen for the moment when the slow tune and the fast figures sound together. Two dances that seemed opposites turn out to fit.

movements.heading: Dance of the Boys
movements.title: Dance of the Boys
movements.summary: The boys’ dance again, faster and wilder, with the chorus. The camp is working itself into a frenzy.

mainIdeas.description: The skipping dance, now with voices and more percussion.

stops.hear: The fast, skipping music returns
The chorus joins in, loud and rhythmic

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden break

notice: Compare it with movement IV. The tune is the same; the voices and the extra weight make it sound like a crowd.

movements.heading: General Dance
movements.title: General Dance
movements.summary: The finale. The men’s wild tune from the second dance and the opening theme return, now in a bright major key, with the full chorus and orchestra. The dances end in a blaze of sound.

mainIdeas.description: Themes from the earlier dances combined in a fast, four-beat finale.

stops.hear: Fast and brilliant, with the whole orchestra
The clarinet’s whirling tune from the men’s dance returns, with the chorus

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Louder and faster, to a final crash

notice: Listen for the men’s wild tune from movement II. It returns here as the engine of the finale.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Beecham made the recording at Abbey Road in November 1956 with his own orchestra and choir. On this album, a 1999 CD reissue, the dances follow his *Scheherazade* as tracks 5–11, divided into seven parts.

threads.title: Two worlds in one camp
threads.body: The captive women’s longing song (I, V) and the warriors’ wild dances (II, IV, VI) belong to the same scene. Borodin keeps them apart at first, then makes them sound together.

threads.title: The East as seen from Russia
threads.body: Curling ornaments, repeated drumming rhythms and bright percussion: Borodin’s picture of the steppe peoples, as imagined by a nineteenth-century Russian, not a record of their real music.

threads.title: A composer with a day job
threads.body: Borodin wrote this music in the time his laboratory left him, and the dances survived only because his friends pushed him to finish them for a concert.
